report_name: US Seizes Chinese Hacking Platforms Targeting Critical Infrastructure

threat_actors.name: QTFY
threat_actors.description: A Chinese state-sponsored hacking group that operated the QScan and QTRouter platforms to target U.S. critical infrastructure. The group is reportedly employed by Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company and provides services to clients including China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) and the People's Liberation Army (PLA).

attack_patterns.name: Vulnerability Scanning
attack_patterns.description: The QScan tool was used for broad, automated scanning of the internet to identify vulnerable Internet of Things (IoT) devices for compromise.

attack_patterns.name: Acquire Infrastructure
attack_patterns.description: The QTFY group acquired infrastructure by compromising thousands of IoT devices to create the QTRouter botnet.

attack_patterns.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
attack_patterns.description: The QTFY group likely exploited known vulnerabilities in public-facing IoT devices to gain initial access and infect them.

attack_patterns.name: Multi-hop Proxy
attack_patterns.description: The QTRouter platform was used as a multi-hop proxy, routing malicious traffic through a network of compromised IoT devices to obfuscate the true origin of attacks.

attack_patterns.name: Web Protocols
attack_patterns.description: The seized domains were part of the command and control infrastructure, likely using web protocols for communication between the malware and C2 servers.

attack_patterns.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
attack_patterns.description: Adversaries may have used downloader utilities like wget or curl on compromised IoT devices to transfer malicious payloads or tools.

malware.name: QScan
malware.description: A malicious platform used by the QTFY group for widespread, automated scanning of the internet to identify and infect vulnerable Internet of Things (IoT) devices, conscripting them into a botnet.

malware.name: QTRouter
malware.description: A malicious platform operated by the QTFY group that served as an obfuscation network. It leveraged a botnet of compromised IoT devices (infected by QScan) as proxy nodes to mask the origin of attacks against U.S. targets.

identities.name: Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company
identities.description: A China-based company that reportedly employs the QTFY hacking group.

identities.name: Ministry of State Security (China)
identities.description: A client of the QTFY hacking group, receiving hacking-as-a-service capabilities.

identities.name: People's Liberation Army
identities.description: A client of the QTFY hacking group, receiving hacking-as-a-service capabilities.

identities.name: National Aeronautics and Space Administration
identities.description: A high-value U.S. entity targeted by the QTFY hacking group.

identities.name: Federal Reserve
identities.description: A high-value U.S. entity targeted by the QTFY hacking group.

identities.name: Department of Energy
identities.description: A high-value U.S. entity targeted by the QTFY hacking group.

identities.name: U.S. Senate
identities.description: A high-value U.S. entity targeted by the QTFY hacking group.

identities.name: U.S. Critical Infrastructure
identities.description: A broad class of targets for the QTFY hacking campaign, including hospitals and power companies.

infrastructure.name: QTRouter Obfuscation Network
infrastructure.description: A network of compromised IoT devices used by QTFY to proxy malicious traffic and hide the origin of attacks.

infrastructure.name: QTFY C2 Domains
infrastructure.description: Internet domains seized by the U.S. government that were used for command and control of the QScan and QTRouter platforms.
